cards.vorderseite: Is the nasal or ear fluid CSF? Confirmatory tests
cards.rueckseite:
- **β2-transferrin:** in CSF (and vitreous) but not in tears, saliva, nasal secretions or serum; ≥ 0.5 mL needed; very sensitive and specific → **test of choice**
- **Glucose:** CSF > 30 mg/dL vs. secretions < 5; a negative test is more useful (45–75% false positives)
- **Halo (double ring) sign:** blood with a clear outer ring on linen; unreliable
- **Reservoir sign:** gush when bending forward after lying down (sphenoid sinus pooling)
- **Pneumocephalus** on CT in ≈ 20%; anosmia in ≈ 5%
- Localization: thin-cut CT; if unclear and actively leaking → **CT cisternography** (intrathecal iohexol). Never intrathecal methylene blue (neurotoxic).

cards.text: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension: incidence {{c1::≈ 5/100,000}}, mostly women in their {{c2::40s}}; CSF opening pressure typically {{c3::< 6 cm H₂O}}, but can be normal. The usual source is a {{c4::spinal}} leak (meningeal diverticulum, ventral dural tear from a disc/osteophyte spur, or CSF–venous fistula), often linked to connective tissue disorders such as {{c5::Marfan or Ehlers–Danlos}}; median diagnostic delay ≈ 4 months.

**Evans index** = maximal width of the frontal horns ÷ maximal {{c1::inner biparietal diameter}} on the same axial slice: 0.2–0.25 normal, 0.25–0.3 borderline, {{c2::> 0.3}} ventricular enlargement. Hydrocephalus is also suggested when both **temporal horns are ≥ {{c3::2 mm}}** wide and the sylvian/interhemispheric fissures and sulci are not visible.

cards.rueckseite:
Enlarged **frontal subarachnoid spaces** in the first year, with **macrocrania** and normal or slightly enlarged ventricles, otherwise normal child.
**Key differential:** chronic subdural collection (including **non-accidental trauma**): the **cortical vein sign** (veins crossing the fluid to the inner table) indicates subarachnoid fluid, not subdural.
**Course:** resolves by 12–18 months (to 2 years) without a shunt; follow head circumference and imaging; repositioning against plagiocephaly.

Mutation of **L1CAM** at **Xq28**; males affected, mothers carriers; ≈ 2% of hydrocephalus.
**Features (CRASH/MASA):** aqueductal stenosis, **adducted (clasped) thumbs** (≈ 50%), spastic paraplegia, intellectual disability, corpus callosum agenesis.
Genetic counseling: 50% of sons of carriers affected.

Fourth ventricle cut off from both the aqueduct and its outlets; occurs in **2–3% of shunted patients**, especially after **post-infectious or post-hemorrhagic** hydrocephalus and repeated shunt infections (aqueduct closes when the lateral ventricles are overdrained).
**Signs:** headache, ataxia, lower cranial nerve dysfunction, **facial diplegia and bilateral VI palsy** (facial colliculus), reduced consciousness.
**Treatment:** fourth ventricular catheter (preferably placed from below the tonsils under vision) linked to the shunt, endoscopic aqueductoplasty, or open fenestration; risk of brainstem injury from the catheter as the ventricle shrinks.

- ≈ 58% of shunted women have raised ICP symptoms in pregnancy (shunt failure, venous engorgement, tumor growth, venous thrombosis); always also exclude **preeclampsia**
- Compare ventricles with a preconception baseline scan; tap the shunt if unchanged
- **Revision:** VP shunt in the 1st–2nd trimester; **VA or ventriculopleural** in the 3rd (avoid the uterus)
- **Delivery:** vaginal if asymptomatic, with a short second stage; symptomatic near term → **C-section under general anesthesia** (no epidural with raised ICP)
- Peripartum antibiotics (coliforms) to prevent shunt infection

**Complications:** **basilar artery** (or PCA/PComm) injury with catastrophic bleeding, hypothalamic injury (hyperphagia), pituitary stalk injury (DI, amenorrhea), transient **III/VI palsies**, fornix injury (memory), late traumatic basilar aneurysm.
**Low success (≈ 20% patent):** tumor, **previous shunt**, previous **SAH** or infection, whole-brain radiation, visible adhesions; also infants < 6 months (immature subarachnoid space).
Best: previously untreated acquired aqueductal stenosis (60–94%).

cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 25.1, p. 453–454. Sum = approximate % chance of ETV success at 6 months. < 40%: poor; ≥ 80%: ETV better than shunt from the start; 50–70%: higher early failure than shunt, but ETV advantage after 3–6 months.

cards.rueckseite:
- Obstruction: **proximal (ventricular catheter) most common**; distal 12–34% (omentum, pseudocyst, adhesions, malposition)
- **Abdominal pseudocyst:** usually infection-related → tap/culture, externalize, treat infection
- **Inguinal hernia (17%)**, hydrocele, scrotal migration, viscus perforation, volvulus
- Overshunting (more than VA, longer siphon column)
- Seizures ≈ 5.5% in year 1 (all ventricular shunts)
- Conduit for extraneural tumor spread (medulloblastoma), silicone allergy (rare)

VA shunt: shunt nephritis, endocarditis, PE, cor pulmonale, needs lengthening with growth.

Overshunting problems in **10–12%** of long-term shunts: slit ventricles, intracranial hypotension (postural headache), **subdural hematomas**, craniosynostosis/microcephaly, aqueductal stenosis.
**Slit ventricles** on CT: 3–80% of shunted patients, mostly asymptomatic.
**Slit ventricle syndrome** (< 12%): intermittent proximal occlusion from collapsed ventricles coapting the catheter; **low ventricular compliance**, so the ventricles stay small even during malfunction; intermittent headaches, vomiting, VI palsy; the valve refills slowly.
**Treatment:** raise valve pressure, **antisiphon device**, revision; in refractory cases ETV, subtemporal decompression or cranial expansion.

cards.vorderseite: Subdural hematoma in a shunted patient
cards.rueckseite:
Caused by overdrainage (brain collapses from the dura, bridging veins tear), especially in older patients with large ventricles and low-pressure valves.
**Management:** small and asymptomatic → observe, raise the valve setting (programmable); symptomatic → evacuate the hematoma **and** prevent recurrence (higher setting, temporary ligation/occlusion of the shunt or antisiphon device), then reopen gradually.

Congenital/childhood aqueductal obstruction that decompensates in adulthood: **macrocephaly** (head circumference > 98th percentile), triventricular hydrocephalus with an empty/expanded sella, and symptoms of raised ICP or NPH-like gait/cognitive decline.
**Treatment:** **ETV** (high success because the obstruction is aqueductal).

cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 509–510. Prevalence ≈ 2–5% (age 6 months to 6 years). ASMs are not indicated (phenobarbital lowered IQ by ≈ 8 points); intermittent diazepam during fever reduces recurrence.

cards.vorderseite: First unprovoked seizure: recurrence and causes
cards.rueckseite:
**Provoked causes:** acute neurologic insult (stroke, trauma, CNS infection), underlying CNS lesion (tumor, AVM, hydrocephalus), metabolic (hypo-/hypernatremia, **hypoglycemia**, hypocalcemia, uremia), drugs/withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines, cocaine, **flumazenil**, cyclosporine), eclampsia.
**After a first unprovoked seizure** ≈ 27–40% recur; higher with family history, **epileptiform EEG**, or remote CNS insult. No recurrence in those seizure-free for 3 years.
Work-up: labs, toxicology, MRI, EEG.

Idiopathic generalized epilepsy, 5–10% of epilepsy, onset in adolescence.
**Three seizure types:** **myoclonic jerks after waking**, generalized tonic-clonic, absences.
**EEG:** generalized **polyspike-and-wave**; photosensitivity; triggered by sleep deprivation and alcohol.
**Treatment:** valproate (levetiracetam/lamotrigine in women of childbearing age); usually **lifelong**. Carbamazepine/phenytoin can worsen it. Not a surgical epilepsy.

Usually considered after **≥ 2 years seizure-free**; ≈ 1/3 relapse, most within the first year (highest risk in the first 3 months of taper).
**Higher relapse risk:** generalized or **secondarily generalized** seizures, many seizures before control, **several drugs needed** (80% relapse if the third drug was needed), **persisting EEG abnormality**, JME, structural lesion.
**Lower risk:** long seizure-free period, monotherapy, normal EEG.

- **Enzyme inducers** (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone; oxcarbazepine/topiramate at high doses) → **oral contraceptive failure** (up to 4×)
- Seizures increase in ≈ 17–30% of pregnancies (falling free levels, nonadherence) → monitor levels (lamotrigine and levetiracetam drop markedly)
- Malformation rate ≈ 4–5% (double the baseline); **valproate** worst (neural tube defects 1–2%, lower IQ); polytherapy more than additive
- Folic acid supplementation; status epilepticus is dangerous for mother and fetus

**Favor NES:** female (≈ 80%), **out-of-phase** limb movements, side-to-side head movements, pelvic thrusting, **eyes closed** with resistance to opening, gradual onset, waxing and waning, long duration, crying/talking during the event, memory of the event, no postictal confusion.
**Favor epileptic:** stereotyped events, eyes open, in-phase clonic movements, tongue bite on the side, incontinence, injury, arising from sleep, postictal confusion, raised **prolactin** 10–20 min after a GTC seizure.
Gold standard: **video-EEG**. Up to 10–30% of NES patients also have epilepsy.

cards.text: Alcohol withdrawal seizures occur {{c1::7–30 h (mostly within 48 h)}} after the last drink, are usually {{c2::generalized, brief and few}}, and do not need long-term antiseizure medication. A {{c3::focal seizure or status epilepticus}} should prompt a search for another cause (e.g., subdural hematoma). Treat withdrawal with {{c4::benzodiazepines}}.

cards.rueckseite:
Pain persisting **> 1 month** after the zoster rash heals; in ≈ **10%** of herpes zoster, mainly **age > 60**, diabetes, **ophthalmic** division (zoster: thoracic ≈ 65%, trigeminal ≈ 20%).
VZV latent in the dorsal root/trigeminal ganglion. Constant burning pain with **allodynia**, dermatomal; unlikely to remit after 6 months.
**Treatment:** antivirals early, gabapentin/pregabalin, tricyclics, topical lidocaine/capsaicin, zoster vaccine for prevention; surgical options (DREZ, stimulation) are disappointing.

- **Type I** (reflex sympathetic dystrophy): no identifiable nerve lesion
- **Type II** (causalgia): after a **nerve injury** (median, ulnar, sciatic most often)

**Features:** burning pain out of proportion, **allodynia**, vasomotor changes (warm/red or cold/blue), sudomotor changes, edema, **trophic** changes (shiny skin, nail/hair changes, stiff joints), patchy osteoporosis. Clinical diagnosis (Budapest criteria); no reliable test.
**Treatment:** early mobilization/physical therapy, neuropathic drugs, sympathetic blocks (lasting relief in only ≈ 18–25%), **spinal cord stimulation**; can follow carpal tunnel or spine surgery.
